sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) represents a heterogeneous group of myeloid neoplasms, with approximately two-thirds identified as lower-risk MDS (LR-MDS). LR-MDS with thrombocytopenia is associated with poor prognosis, a high risk of life-threatening hemorrhage, and limited treatment options.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We explored a prospective single-arm, single-center study on the combination of very-low-dose decitabine (VLD-DAC, 3.5 mg/m2/day from days 1 to 5 of a 28-day cycle) and recombinant human thrombopoietin (rhTPO, 1.5 million units/day from days 1 to 14) for treating LR-MDS with thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 50 × 109/L). The primary endpoint was the hematologic improvement-platelet (HI-P) rate.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Among 20 patients, 19 completed at least two treatment cycles. Of these, 63% (12/19) achieved HI-P within 1 month (range, 0.7 to 3.5 months), 57% (4/7) of patients gained platelet transfusion independence. Furthermore, 74% (14/19) demonstrated hematologic response in at least one blood cell lineage, with 86% (6/7) achieving independent of red blood cell transfusions. During treatment, no patients experienced disease progression, but later, 2 patients did, and both ultimately succumbed. The main adverse reactions encountered during treatment were neutropenia and infection. Additionally, 2 patients succumbed to complications arising from hemorrhage or severe infection.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Real-world results indicate that VLD-DAC combined with rhTPO ameliorates thrombocytopenia in LR-MDS, potentially enhances patient prognosis, and demonstrates a favorable safety profile.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) is a clonal myeloid neoplasm characterized by morphologic bone marrow dysplasia, ineffective hematopoiesis leading to peripheral blood cytopenias, and a high risk of progressing to leukemia [1, 2]. MDS is stratified into lower-risk and higher-risk categories based on prognostic assessments. Treatment for lower-risk MDS (LR-MDS) focuses on improving blood cell levels and quality of life, while treatment for higher-risk MDS (HR-MDS) aims to delay leukemia progression and extend survival [1–3]. Approximately two-thirds of MDS patients are classified as lower-risk, including those with International Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS) low risk or intermediate risk-1, while 25% face rapid disease progression and a survival expectancy of less than two years [4]. Thrombocytopenia is a significant complication in LR-MDS, associated with an elevated risk of hemorrhage, disease progression, and poor prognosis [5–7].

LR-MDS typically presents as refractory anemia, but over 10% of patients experience severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count < 30 × 109/L) [8, 9], which delays the treatment of MDS and heightens the risk of life-threatening bleeding [5, 10]. The predominant therapeutic approach involves platelet transfusions, but has drawbacks like transfusion reactions, ineffective platelet transfusion, and economic burden [11]. For LR-MDS patients with thrombocytopenia, thrombopoietin receptor agonists (TPO-RAs), [12] such as eltrombopag and romiplostim, offer potential treatment options, demonstrating overall response rates (ORRs) of approximately 40–50% [9, 13] and hematologic improvement-platelet (HI-P) rates of 30–40% [5, 9, 14]. However, these treatments may temporarily increase blasts and the risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) [15, 16]. Other options include hypomethylating agents (HMAs) [17], immunosuppressants, and androgens [18, 19], but there is currently no approved treatment for thrombocytopenia in LR-MDS [5], underscoring the urgent need for novel and effective therapeutic strategies.

HMAs improve hematologic function in 30%−40% of HR-MDS patients [20]. For LR-MDS, reduced doses of HMAs have been attempted [21–23], such as azacitidine (AZA, 75 mg/m2/day) or decitabine (DAC, 20 mg/m2/day) over 3 days every 28 days, achieving ORRs of 49% and 70%, respectively [21]. Decitabine shows better outcomes in transfusion independence, cytogenetic improvement, and time-free survival [24]. In LR-MDS patients with high-risk factors, including transfusion dependency, cytopenia, elevated bone marrow blasts, and adverse cytogenetics, the benefits of DAC over AZA are more pronounced [25].

Thrombocytopenia in MDS primarily arises from ineffective platelet production, with contributions from immune-mediated destruction and dysfunction [10]. In certain cases, isolated thrombocytopenia in MDS must be distinguished from other non-clonal disorders, such as immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) [26]. Given the myelosuppressive effects of decitabine, we opted for a very-low-dose regimen to manage thrombocytopenia in patients with LR-MDS, a method shown to boost platelet levels in ITP [27]. Thrombopoietin (TPO), which is crucial for platelet production, binds to the thrombopoietin receptor (TPO-R) on the surfaces of megakaryocytes [9] and is approved to treat ITP and chemotherapy-induced thrombocytopenia. Thus, we conducted a single-center, single-arm prospective study combining very-low-dose decitabine (VLD-DAC) with recombinant human thrombopoietin (rhTPO) to enhance platelet levels and retard disease progression in LR-MDS.

sec.title: Patients and eligibility
sec.p: Data were collected from patients diagnosed with LR-MDS who were treated with VLD-DAC and rhTPO between April 10, 2021, and June 10, 2024. The inclusion criteria for the study were as follows: (1) patients aged 14 years or older with MDS as per the World Health Organization (WHO) 2022 classification [28], (2) a platelet count of 50 × 109/L or less at the initiation of DAC and rhTPO treatment, (3) classified as low-risk or intermediate-1 risk according to the IPSS based on the 2008 WHO classification [29], and (4) an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (ECOG PS) of 0 to 2. The exclusion criteria for the study were as follows: (1) more than 5% bone marrow blast cells at screening, (2) isolated deletion of chromosome 5q [del(5q)] with or without one additional cytogenetic abnormality, excluding monosomy 7 or deletion of chromosome 7q [del(7q)], (3) presence of grade 2 or grade 3 myelofibrosis (MF), (4) previous administration of rhTPO or TPO-RAs before enrollment in this study, (5) presence of uncontrolled intercurrent illness, (6) active or uncontrolled infection, (7) an estimated survival time of less than three months, and (8) pregnancy or breastfeeding.

This study utilizes data from the National Longitudinal Cohort of Hematological Diseases in China (NICHE, NCT04645199). The trial was conducted in compliance with the principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and received approval from the ethics committees at the Institute of Hematology and Blood Diseases Hospital (approval no. IIT2021029-EC-1). Informed written consent was obtained from all participating patients.

sec.title: Treatment regimen
sec.p:
VLD-DAC was administered at a dose of 3.5 mg/m2/day via a 5-h continuous intravenous infusion on days 1–5 of a 28-day cycle. rhTPO was routinely administered subcutaneously at a dose of 1.5 million units per day from day 1 to day 14, concurrently with DAC administration (Fig. 1). The 28-day interval between decitabine treatments allowed most patients to reach nadir values for hemoglobin, platelets, and absolute neutrophil count (ANC), facilitating hematologic recovery prior to the subsequent treatment cycle. Adjustments, including delays or discontinuation of VLD-DAC and rhTPO treatment, were implemented as necessary. If grade 3 or 4 non-hematological adverse events occurred in patients during treatment cycles, the administration of the treatment was suspended until the condition stabilized.Fig. 1
Trial profile. DAC for decitabine. rhTPO for recombinant human thrombopoietin

In cases where the patient did not achieve a clinical response following two cycles of treatment, alternative therapeutic regimens were implemented. Conversely, patients who responded to the initial treatment had the option to proceed with allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT), continue with consolidation therapy with the same regimen, or adopt a watchful waiting approach. The duration of consolidation therapy was determined by the occurrence of disease relapse, disease progression, withdrawal of consent, intercurrent illness, or the emergence of severe adverse events, as assessed by the investigators. Blood transfusions, granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF), antimicrobial agents, and antifungal therapies were administered based on the clinical judgment of the attending physicians.

sec.title: Clinical response and safety
sec.p: The primary outcome measured was the platelet response, defined as HI-P for patients with a baseline platelet count over 20 × 109/L, the count rises by at least 30 × 109/L; for those with a baseline platelet count under 20 × 109/L, the count increases to over 20 × 109/L and at least doubles without platelet transfusion, which was evaluated during the first 2 to 4 cycles in accordance with the modified International Working Group 2006 criteria [30]. Secondary outcomes encompassed: (1) the median onset time of HI-P, (2) the median duration of response (DoR) of HI-P, (3) other hematologic responses, including HI-erythroid (HI-E) and HI-neutrophil (HI-N), and (4) transfusion independence, and (5) overall survival (OS). Overall survival (OS) was quantified as the duration in months from the initiation of therapy to the date of death. Adverse events were evaluated in accordance with the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE), Version 5.0.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Patients who received at least one dose of VLD-DAC + rhTPO in the extension study were included in the safety analysis cohort. Safety data, along with demographic and baseline characteristics, were summarized using descriptive statistics, including means, medians, and ranges, for all participants. Graphical representations were generated using GraphPad Prism software version 9.1.1 and R Studio.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p:
A cohort of 20 patients who met the inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria was enrolled in the study and treated with VLD-DAC and rhTPO between April 10, 2021, and June 10, 2024. One patient withdrew after receiving only one cycle of decitabine combination with rhTPO then proceeded to HSCT. The baseline characteristics of the remaining 19 patients available for data analysis are listed in Table 1. Among these 19 patients, 8 were male and 11 were female, with a median age of 51 years (range, 17 to 77 years). Of these, 79% (15 out of 19) had previously undergone one or more treatments, including erythropoietin (EPO), TPO-RAs, demethylating agents, immunosuppressants, immunomodulators, and androgens. Additionally, five patients (26%) presented with secondary MDS from aplastic anemia. At screening, the bone marrow blast percentage for all patients was below 5%. Among them, 3 patients initially diagnosed with myelodysplastic syndrome with excess blasts-1 (MDS-IB1) or MDS-IB2 achieved marrow complete remission (mCR) after treatment with BCL2 inhibitor plus azacitidine but continued to have persistent cytopenia. All patients were classified as intermediate 1-risk MDS according to the IPSS score, 63% (12/19) had intermediate-risk MDS by the IPSS-R [31], and 63% had high or very high-risk MDS by the IPSS-M [32]. The median platelet count was 28 × 109/L (range, 2 to 48 × 109/L), with 53% (10/19) of patients having counts below 30 × 109/L and 37% (7/19) below 20 × 109/L needing platelet transfusions. The median hemoglobin was 55 g/L (range 28 to 110 g/L), and 63% (12/19) required red blood cell transfusions. sec.title: Response and outcome
sec.p:
Nineteen patients completed a median of 4 treatment courses (range 2 to 11 courses), with 63% (12/19) of the patients achieving HI-P. Notably, 57% (4/7) of the patients dependent on platelet transfusions became transfusion-free. The median time to onset of HI-P was 1 month (range, 0.7 to 3.5 months), and the median DoR of HI-P was 2.25 months (range, 1 to 7 months) (Fig. 2). Patient 4 achieved HI-P rapidly, one month post-treatment, but lost it after four.Fig. 2
Swimmer plot of dynamic response and events of the 19 patients. Each bar represents one individual patient. Different colors and shapes coded by different response and events. Dark red triangles represent HI-P, dark blue circles represent HI-E. The lighter color of red triangle and blue circle indicate loss of efficacy. HSCT denotes hematopoietic stem cell transplantation

months. The patient subsequently regained HI-P efficacy three months later with continued treatment, which was sustained for an additional three months. The median platelet count among the 12 patients achieving HI-P showed an increase after both one and four courses of treatment (Fig. 3). At best response, the median platelet count for these 12 patients was 90 × 109/L (range, 24 to 142 × 109/L). Furthermore, 14 patients (74%) exhibited at least one lineage of blood cell response, including HI-P, HI-E, or HI-N, with 8 cases (42%) achieving HI-E and 3 cases (16%) achieving HI-N. Notably, among the 7 patients who were reliant on red blood cell transfusions, 6 cases (86%) achieved transfusion independence.Fig. 3
Median (25th [Q1] and 75th [Q3] percentiles) platelet counts for 12 HI-P patients by study course and month

Over a median follow-up of 6.5 months (range, 1.5 to 33.75 months), one patient progressed to MDS-IB1 after 4 months, and another to AML after 18 months. Additionally, three patients underwent allo-HSCT (Fig. 2). The median OS has not yet been reached. Of the 19 patients, one died from cerebral hemorrhage 4 months post-treatment, another from severe complications at 5 months, two from disease progression at 5.75 months and 18 months, and one from a coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) at 21 months.

Of the 3 patients with cytogenetic evaluation, 2 achieved complete cytogenetic remission (CyCR) and 1 attained partial cytogenetic remission (CyPR). Figure 4 illustrates the baseline genetic traits of patients according to platelet response. Targeted next-generation sequencing revealed somatic mutations commonly associated with myeloid neoplasia in 84% (16 out of 19) of patients, with a median of 2 hotspot mutations per patient (range, 0 to 6 mutations). The most prevalent mutation type identified was splicing, occurring in 62.5% (10 out of 16) of cases, including SF3B1, U2AF1, ZRSR2, SRSF2, and PRPF8. The next most frequent mutations, each with a 25% (4/16) incidence, were transcription (NPM1, RUNX1), DNA methylation (DNMT3A, TET2, IDH2), signal transduction (NRAS, GNAS, CBL1), and histone modification (ASXL1, BCOR). A few patients had RNA helicases, oncogene/anti-oncogene, and other mutations. Among the 8 patients assessed for molecular genetic alterations after 4 courses of treatment, one lost U2AF1 and GNAS mutations post-treatment, another lost NPM1 and BCOR mutations, while the remaining 6 showed no significant changes in their mutational profiles.Fig. 4

sec.title: Safety
sec.p:
During treatment, 13 patients experienced adverse reactions. One patient died from intracranial hemorrhage, while another succumbed to a severe lung infection and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Common grade 3 or grade 4 non-hematological adverse reactions included infection, bleeding, and fatigue. Neutropenia was the primary hematological issue, potentially contributing to the heightened risk of infection. Two patients had grade 1 or grade 2 alanine aminotransferase elevation, and one experienced heart failure. Notably, all adverse reactions classified as grade 4 or lower were recoverable. Furthermore, seven patients successfully completed the treatment without any adverse reactions. All adverse events are listed in Table 2. sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In patients with LR-MDS and severe thrombocytopenia, 17% experienced disease progression to AML, with a 5-year survival rate of 58.1%.9 Treatment options for MDS accompanied by thrombocytopenia remain limited, and their safety profiles are uncertain. A study combining AZA and eltrombopag in higher-risk MDS did not reduce platelet transfusions and showed a trend toward AML progression [33]. Another study examined very low-dose decitabine (6 mg/m2/day for seven consecutive days, repeated every four weeks) in intermediate- and high-risk MDS, achieving a 67.7% ORR, with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia as the primary adverse reactions [34]. Consequently, we employed a regimen of VLD-DAC in combination with rhTPO to potentially enhance platelet levels and delay disease progression.

In this study, we used a much lower dose of decitabine than typically used for MDS due to two primary considerations. Firstly, to ensure safety and minimize cytotoxic effects. Secondly, the dosage was aligned with the low dose decitabine protocol utilized in the treatment of patients with ITP, which markedly improves platelet levels [27]. The potential mechanisms underlying this improvement include the promotion of megakaryocyte differentiation, inhibition of cytotoxic T cell activity, enhancement of regulatory T cell function, and immunomodulatory functions [27, 35, 36]. The subsequent phase involves conducting a thorough exploration of the mechanisms underlying the responders and non-responders to VLD-DAC and rhTPO combined treatment in LR-MDS with thrombocytopenia.

Our study found that combining very-low-dose decitabine with rhTPO effectively treated lower-risk MDS with thrombocytopenia, achieving favorable hematological remission. Notably, nearly two-thirds of the patients exhibited significant improvements in platelet counts, which reduced the risk of severe hemorrhagic events, with no rapid disease progression was observed. Neutropenia and infection were common adverse reactions requiring timely attention and intervention. Simultaneously, adverse events such as fatigue, hemorrhage, heart failure, and liver damage were observed, particularly in patients with ineffective treatment; however, these conditions are generally manageable. In patients with LR-MDS who respond effectively to VLD-DAC combined with rhTPO, there is a significant improvement in quality of life by eliminating platelet transfusions, thereby offering the potential for subsequent curative intervention through allo-HSCT.

Despite the availability of TPO-RAs and other therapies, effective treatments for thrombocytopenia in LR-MDS are limited, posing a clinical challenge. New strategies, such as novel growth factors and combination therapies, are under investigation to boost platelet response, reduce bleeding risk, and improve patient outcomes. However, the clinical data on rhTPO are limited, with its use mainly approved in China, which restricts the generalizability of our findings. This study is constrained by its small sample size, single-arm design lacking a control group, and limited research duration. The median duration of platelet response in this study was short, likely due to the limited sample size and brief follow-up, indicating a need for further research to evaluate the durability and clinical significance of these responses. Another limitation of this study is the diverse study population, which includes previously treated patients, secondary MDS from aplastic anemia, and classification inconsistencies between conventional lower-risk and IPSS-M higher-risk groups. Additionally, this study relies on purely descriptive statistical analysis, which restricts definitive conclusions about efficacy. This exploratory study, with a small sample size and no control group, offers preliminary, hypothesis-generating results. Although the platelet responses seem promising, the short follow-up and diverse patient population limit the generalizability of the findings. Therefore, further research through multi-center, large-sample, randomized controlled studies is essential to substantiate the long-term efficacy, survival outcomes, adverse effects, and disease evolution, including clonal evolution, bone marrow fibrosis, and disease progression.

In conclusion, very-low-dose decitabine combined with rhTPO effectively and safely raises platelet levels in lower-risk MDS with thrombocytopenia. Further randomized controlled studies with larger sample sizes are necessary to substantiate the novel solution.
